items.title: The ELIZA effect
items.claim: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA chatbot (1966) used simple keyword matching. What was Weizenbaum's reaction when his secretary engaged emotionally with it?

options.text: He was thrilled and commercialised it
He became a sharp critic of attributing understanding to machines

items.reveal_title: ELIZA's creator turned into one of AI's earliest critics
items.reveal:
Weizenbaum's 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason argued against using computers in roles requiring human judgement.

The 'ELIZA effect' describes the human tendency to attribute understanding to systems that have none.
items.why: Creators often see clearly what users want to project. The pattern recurs with each new generation of chatbots.

items.title: Snowden disclosures revealed bulk metadata collection
items.claim: Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures revealed extensive intelligence programmes. Which is most accurate about PRISM?

options.text: PRISM was a programme for monitoring weather data
PRISM was a US National Security Agency programme collecting communications data from major US tech firms (Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, Facebook, Apple and others) under FISA Section 702

items.reveal:
The Guardian and Washington Post published Snowden's disclosures from June 2013. They revealed PRISM, XKeyscore, Tempora (GCHQ) and Bullrun (NSA's programme to weaken commercial encryption).

The disclosures drove industry-wide adoption of stronger encryption defaults (HTTPS-by-default, end-to-end encrypted messaging) and legal changes (USA Freedom Act 2015 ended bulk telephony metadata collection). The European Court of Justice's Schrems II ruling (2020) invalidated EU-US data transfer arrangements partly citing US surveillance.

Snowden remains in Russia, granted citizenship 2022.
items.why: The architecture of communications systems shapes what surveillance is possible. End-to-end encryption design was reshaped by the disclosures.
